summary: Psalm 145 opens with a personal vow to praise God the King forever, then widens into a chorus where generations speak of God's works, goodness, and righteousness. The center of the psalm describes Yahweh's gracious character, everlasting kingdom, care for the fallen, provision for every living thing, nearness to those who call, and judgment on the wicked. It ends by returning to the speaker's own mouth and calling all flesh to bless Yahweh's holy name.
whyItMatters: Near the end of the Psalter, this chapter helps turn the book toward its final sequence of praise. It gathers many of the book's major claims about God's rule, mercy, provision, and righteousness into one sustained hymn.

context.author: The heading says, "A praise psalm by David." In Psalms, Davidic headings are ancient parts of the transmitted collection, but readers differ over whether they always mark authorship, association, dedication, or collection identity.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and praise.
context.date: Psalms is a many-period anthology; individual poems may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period, and one date for the whole book would be misleading.
context.setting: Psalm 145 stands in Book V of Psalms, the final major section, where the collection moves toward total praise.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew praise poetry. Psalm 145 is one of the psalms shaped as an alphabetic acrostic, a Hebrew feature ordinary English translation does not visibly preserve.

outline.heading: A personal vow to praise the King
outline.note: The speaker addresses God as King, promises daily and everlasting praise, and declares Yahweh's greatness beyond searching.

outline.heading: Praise passed from one generation to another
outline.note: The psalm moves from the speaker's praise to communal testimony about God's works, mighty acts, goodness, and righteousness.

outline.heading: Yahweh's goodness to all his works
outline.note: The poem names Yahweh as gracious, merciful, slow to anger, good to all, and thanked by all his works.

outline.heading: The glory of an everlasting kingdom
outline.note: God's people speak of the kingdom's glory and power, and the psalm says God's dominion endures through all generations.

outline.heading: Care for the fallen and provision for every living thing
outline.note: Yahweh upholds those who fall, raises the bowed down, gives food in due season, and satisfies living creatures.

outline.heading: Nearness, rescue, preservation, and judgment
outline.note: The psalm says Yahweh is righteous and gracious, near to those who call in truth, saving those who fear him, preserving those who love him, and destroying the wicked.

outline.heading: A final summons for all flesh to bless
outline.note: The speaker's own mouth will praise Yahweh, and all flesh is invited to bless his holy name forever.

keyVerses.text: Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised! His greatness is unsearchable.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the central reason for the psalm's praise: Yahweh's greatness exceeds full human measurement.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and of great loving kindness.
keyVerses.why: This compact description anchors the psalm's picture of God's character before it describes God's goodness to all.

keyVerses.text: Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. Your dominion endures throughout all generations. Yahweh is faithful in all his words, and loving in all his deeds.
keyVerses.why: This verse joins the kingdom theme with God's faithfulness and love, making it a hinge between praise of God's reign and praise of God's care.

keyVerses.text: You open your hand, and satisfy the desire of every living thing.
keyVerses.why: This line gives one of the psalm's clearest images of provision: God's open hand meeting the needs of living creatures.

themes: works and mighty acts remembered across generations
care for those who fall and call

questions.question: Who is speaking in Psalm 145?
questions.answer: The heading calls it "A praise psalm by David," and the poem itself speaks in the first person: "I will exalt you" and "I will praise your name." In the Psalms, headings are ancient parts of the received collection, but readers differ over whether every Davidic heading functions as a modern author byline or as a broader association with David.

questions.question: Why does the psalm call God "the King"?
questions.answer: The opening addresses God as "my God, the King," and the middle of the psalm speaks of God's kingdom, power, dominion, and rule through all generations. The chapter is not describing a human throne; it presents Yahweh's reign as everlasting and worthy of public praise.

questions.question: What does "unsearchable" mean here?
questions.answer: In this verse, "unsearchable" describes Yahweh's greatness. The point is not that nothing can be said about God, since the whole psalm says many things; it means God's greatness is beyond being fully searched out or exhausted by human praise.

questions.question: What is happening when one generation tells another?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says one generation commends God's works to another and declares God's mighty acts. The poem imagines praise as something handed on, not kept private, so memory and testimony become part of worship.

questions.question: Does "Yahweh is good to all" mean everyone in the psalm has the same outcome?
questions.answer: No. Verse 9 says Yahweh is good to all and that his tender mercies are over all his works, and verses 15-16 describe provision for every living thing. But verse 20 also says Yahweh preserves those who love him and destroys the wicked, so the psalm holds broad mercy and moral judgment together.

questions.question: Who are "your saints" in verse 10?
questions.answer: The verse places "your saints" alongside "all your works": all God's works give thanks, and God's saints extol him. From this chapter alone, the phrase points to people who belong to God in praise, but the verse does not pause to define the group more narrowly.

questions.question: What does the psalm say God does for vulnerable people?
questions.answer: Verse 14 says Yahweh upholds all who fall and raises those who are bowed down. The following verses also describe food in due season and an open hand satisfying every living thing, so care for weakness and provision for life stand together.

questions.question: Is verse 18 saying every prayer is answered automatically?
questions.answer: Verse 18 says Yahweh is near to all who call on him, specifically "to all who call on him in truth." Verse 19 adds that he hears the cry of those who fear him and saves them. The psalm presents God as near and responsive, but it does not turn prayer into a mechanical formula.

questions.question: Why does the last verse mention "all flesh"?
questions.answer: The psalm begins with the speaker's personal vow to praise and ends by widening the call to "all flesh." That phrase fits the chapter's broad movement: all works, all generations, all who fall, all who call, and every living thing are drawn into the scope of God's rule and praise.

glossary.def: Speech or song that honors Yahweh. In this chapter, praise is both personal and public, daily and everlasting.
A royal title used for God in verse 1. The rest of the psalm develops this by speaking about God's kingdom, power, dominion, and rule through all generations.
God's actions or created order as the psalm presents them. God's works are remembered and covered by tender mercies; they also give thanks to him.
A phrase in verse 8 describing Yahweh's generous and merciful character. The chapter connects it with being gracious, merciful, and slow to anger.
Rule or authority. Verse 13 says God's dominion endures throughout all generations.
A broad expression for living humanity. The final verse calls all flesh to bless Yahweh's holy name forever and ever.
